Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Summary: Short history of dysuria with suprapubic discomfort, brief gross hematuria, and malodorous urine in an otherwise healthy young woman; no fever, flank pain, N/V, or systemic features. Sexually active with a relatively new partner; uses condoms; no vaginal discharge; never screened for STIs. Allergy to clindamycin (swelling).  
- Differential considerations consistent with DDx:  
  - Acute uncomplicated cystitis: Most consistent given dysuria, suprapubic discomfort, hematuria, and lack of systemic signs.  
  - Urethritis due to STI (e.g., Chlamydia/Gonorrhea/Mycoplasma): Consider given new partner and no prior STI screening, though absence of discharge and presence of hematuria favor cystitis.  
  - Vaginitis (BV/Trichomonas) causing external dysuria: Less likely without discharge/pruritus; odor alone is nonspecific.  
- Working diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (acute lower UTI).  
- Plan from visit: Prescribed antibiotic for 3 days—nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim; one tablet twice daily for 3 days (specific agent not documented). Advise increased oral fluids; cranberry juice may help symptoms. Safety-net: return/call if not improved by end of week or sooner for fever, back/flank pain, or feeling more unwell (concern for ascending infection). Advised to avoid sexual activity until symptoms clear and to continue condom use.  
- Considerations (from DDx, not ordered at this visit): If symptoms persist, recur, or are atypical, consider urine testing (dipstick/culture) and STI NAAT screening (chlamydia/gonorrhea +/- Mycoplasma), and pelvic exam if discharge or vaginal symptoms develop.  
- Conflicts: Patient age 19 years (this template is for adults 55+). LMP timing noted as “couple of weeks” vs clinician’s “three weeks.” Antibiotic choice unspecified (nitrofurantoin vs trimethoprim).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Acute uncomplicated cystitis (High): Classic short-duration dysuria with suprapubic discomfort and brief hematuria without systemic features.  
- Urethritis due to STI (Medium): New partner, no prior STI screen, and dysuria without frequency/urgency can indicate urethritis despite lack of discharge.  
- Vaginitis (BV/Trichomonas) causing external dysuria (Low-Medium): Odor noted, but absence of discharge/pruritus and presence of hematuria make this less likely.
